spots.name: Souq Waqif
spots.label: Souq Waqif

text.geographic_location: Souq Waqif is in the Al Souq district in the centre of Doha, a short way inland from the Corniche and Souq Waqif Park.
text.description: Souq Waqif is a traditional marketplace in central Doha, and one of the easiest places in the city to fill a phone gallery. Its low, earth-coloured buildings, timber beams, lanterns and busy lanes sell spices, garments, handicrafts and souvenirs, with plenty of cafés and restaurants in between. The name means 'the standing market', because traders once set up at the gates to show off their wares. The original buildings date from the late 19th or early 20th century. After a fire in 2003 the souq was rebuilt, with the work finished in 2008 and the aim of keeping its old look. The best-known single frame is from the road in front of the souq. A passing car adds a little movement. Inside, the lantern-lit alleys give neat symmetrical views, and the lights glow blue and yellow after dark. The golden thumb sculpture in the middle of the souq also makes a good subject, with the crowd behind it. Ask before photographing people, and leave out government buildings, security staff and anyone praying.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or similar stops listed for this spot, so go by taxi or on foot to the Al Souq district in central Doha and ask for Souq Waqif or Jassim Bin Mohammed Street. From there the middle of the souq is about 340 m, roughly a 4-5 minute walk east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The street viewpoint is a public road, but shops and venues inside the souq may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the lantern-lit alleys and to 2x-3x if your phone has telephoto, to bring the tower closer to the souq frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jassim Bin Mohammed Street (across the road from the souq, looking east toward the Fanar). The souq frontage in the foreground with the spiral tower of the Abdullah Bin Zaid Al Mahmoud Islamic Cultural Center in the background, ideally with a passing car for motion. Across the road from the souq, and face east toward the Fanar. The souq frontage fills the foreground and the spiral tower of the Abdullah Bin Zaid Al Mahmoud Islamic Cultural Center rises behind it. For a balanced picture, line yourself up with the mosque.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the souq frontage to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. After dark in the alleys, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post. Live Photos can catch the passing car.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, midday and late afternoon give similar light on the street view. Early morning is quieter inside the souq, while the alleys look their best in the evening when the lanterns and coloured lights come on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on the central vertical line so the souq frontage sits evenly on either side. Wait for a car to pass through the frame for a touch of motion. For a second picture, go into the souq and shoot straight down a lantern-lit alley so the walls run symmetrically to the centre.

spots.name: National Museum of Qatar
spots.label: National Museum Qatar

text.geographic_location: The museum stands at the south end of Doha's Corniche, rising from the sea and linked to the shore by bridges.
text.description:
The National Museum of Qatar is the big, sculptural building at the south end of Doha's Corniche. French architect Jean Nouvel took the desert rose crystal as his inspiration, and the result is a cluster of 539 interlocking discs rising from the water's edge. At its heart sits the restored early-20th-century palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani. The current building opened on 28 March 2019, on the site of the earlier museum from 1975.

It sits within a wider raised panorama that also takes in Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. That makes it a good spot for a photo that shows the museum in its setting, and for finding a quieter angle than the ground-level views.

The discs are sand-coloured, so the building looks best when the light is soft and low. If you want the close-up shots, the museum grounds are the alternative: the discs glowing warmly near sunset, or the Qatari flag on its pole set against the architecture. Take a few frames from here first, then decide whether to walk over.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach Box Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The museum has its own opening days and photography rules (including limits on flash, tripods and selfie sticks), so check the official site before you go, and check the Box Park viewpoint is open as well.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full panorama with the stadium and MIA Park. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the museum's discs closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the museum very small, so use it only if you want lots of surrounding skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Box Park (upper floors). A raised panoramic view that takes in the National Museum of Qatar along with the Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. The museum lies to the south, and the view also takes in Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. Stand at the side of the floor that faces south and keep clear of anything in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum on screen to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sand-coloured discs keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out. Hold still when using the telephoto, and rest your elbows on a ledge if there is one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset, when the discs can pick up a warm glow. Avoid the harsh midday light, which flattens the building's shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the museum on one of the thirds, leaving the stadium or park to balance the other side. Hold the phone level so the horizon stays straight. For a different view, panorama mode works well for the full sweep. If you later visit the museum itself, look for the discs glowing at sunset, or the Qatari flag against the building.

spots.alt: National Museum of Qatar, Doha: the big, sculptural building at the south end of Doha's Corniche. Photo spot

spots.name: Museum of Islamic Art
spots.label: Museum of Islamic Art

text.geographic_location: On the Corniche waterfront in Doha, at the Dhow Harbour end, looking across the water to the Museum of Islamic Art on its island beside MIA Park, about 2.5 km to the east.
text.description:
The Museum of Islamic Art sits on its own island at one end of Doha's seven-kilometre Corniche, close to the old dhow harbour. Architect I. M. Pei asked for a stand-alone island so that nothing could be built right up against it later. The museum stands on an artificial peninsula about 60 metres off the Corniche, and a crescent-shaped park wraps around it. Pei chose creamy limestone for the outer walls so the stone shows different shades through the day.

The classic view is from the waterfront on Al Corniche, looking across the water. Depending on where you stand, palms may appear in the foreground and the West Bay towers may appear in the background. The museum opened to the public on 8 December 2008 and reopened after a major renovation in October 2022.

On a phone, keep the museum in the middle of the frame and let the water fill the foreground. A little zoom helps to tighten the framing on the museum. If you have time, there are two other good frames. The museum's facade shows a close, symmetrical view with the fountain reflected on the wet paving. MIA Park shows the museum framed by palms and lawns, with the towers behind.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a taxi or walk to the Dhow Harbour end of the Corniche. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The Corniche waterfront is a public space with no ticket needed, but for the museum galleries and any photography rules inside, check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the water, the shoreline and the distant museum together. Then use a little zoom to tighten the framing on the museum. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer, for the facade and fountain frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Corniche (stand east of the Dhow Harbour skyline viewpoint at the northern tip of the harbour, facing the museum across the water). The museum on its island across the water, framed by palms, with the West Bay towers in the background. East of the Dhow Harbour skyline viewpoint at the northern tip of the harbour, and face the museum across the water. Palms and the West Bay towers may appear in the view, depending on where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale limestone does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour into the night, or sunset. Whether sunrise or sunset gives the better light is best checked on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the museum on one of the vertical lines, with the water filling the lower third. If palms are nearby, let a few fronds frame one edge of the picture. For a different view, the museum facade shows the fountain reflected on the wet paving in a close, symmetrical frame, and MIA Park shows the museum with palms and lawns in front.

spots.alt: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha: photo spot
